Lauren / team,

Quick legal read: the proposed 9‑month phasing is acceptable from a drafting standpoint but two edits I recommend to reduce downstream ambiguity:  
1) Replace “clawback” with a defined term “Rebate Reversal” and spell out the exact calculation (we should reference the same usage metric used for invoicing to prevent disputes).
2) Add a 30‑day notice and cure period before any reversal is assessed; without a notice period Acme can get surprised by retroactive charges which often stalls renewals.

I tracked those changes in the PDF and left a short comment asking Finance whether the 60/30/10 split is payable by invoice credit or direct refund — that affects revenue recognition.

I defer to Karthik on whether we can accept the 9‑month schedule from a commercial perspective (vs. 12).

— Irene

All —

Commercial sanity check: moving to 9 months is doable provided Acme accepts a modest taper to the effective rebate (we should preserve the yearly headline CPM threshold that triggers the highest rebate bucket). Proposed concession: 9‑month phasing with the following guardrails —  
- Annualized commit floor still applies; if annualized usage drops below 85% of committed volume within the 12‑month period, rebate reversal applies pro rata.
- Maintain monthly uplift application (as Lauren stated) but cap uplift credits to a maximum monthly token delta to limit tail risk.

Ben — I flagged the worksheet to show impact at 3 assumed ramp profiles (fast/medium/slow). If any of those create negative unit economics we should tighten the taper (e.g., 70/20/10 instead of 60/30/10).

Karthik Iyer
Director, Commercial Programs | Redwood Inference
